source: Snapshot and History Graphs
A y–x graph shows the whole wave at one instant; a y–t graph follows one point over time.
Students read the wavelength off a y–t graph, which really shows the period.

A wave changes in both space and time, but a graph has only one horizontal axis. So there are two kinds of wave graph, and reading the wrong one is a classic mistake. Both are pictures of the same wave.

A snapshot graph ($y$ against $x$) shows the whole wave at one instant: read the wavelength $\lambda$ between crests. A history graph ($y$ against $t$) follows one point over time: read the period $T$ between crests. Both show the amplitude $A$. Then $\role[wave speed]{velocity}{v} = \role{wavelength}{\lambda}/\role[period]{time}{T} = \role{frequency}{f}\role{wavelength}{\lambda}$.
The snapshot graph freezes time; the history graph freezes position and watches the marked point bob up and down.

Why does the history graph look like a backward copy of the snapshot? For a wave moving to the right, the part of the wave just to the left of a point is what arrives there next. So the point's future displacements are the wave shape read from right to left. The two graphs have the same shape but different axes, with distance on one and time on the other, linked by $x = vt$.

Reading the "wavelength" off a $y$–$t$ graph. The distance between crests on a history graph is a time, the period $T$, measured in seconds. Check the axis label and the units: meters means wavelength, seconds means period.

A snapshot graph of a wave shows crests $0.40\ \text{m}$ apart and a height of $3.0\ \text{cm}$ above the center line. A history graph of one point shows crests $0.050\ \text{s}$ apart. Find $A$, $\lambda$, $T$, $f$ and $v$.
Reading two graphs
Amplitude: $A = 3.0\ \text{cm}$ (from the center line, not crest to trough).
Wavelength from the snapshot: $\lambda = 0.40\ \text{m}$. Period from the history: $T = 0.050\ \text{s}$.
$f = \dfrac{1}{T} = 20\ \text{Hz}$, and $v = \dfrac{\lambda}{T} = \dfrac{0.40}{0.050} = 8.0\ \text{m/s}$.
A wave moves to the right. On the snapshot graph, a point sits on the rising slope just before a crest (the crest is to its right). Is that point moving up or down right now?
Which way is it moving?
Down
The wave moves right, so the shape just to the point's left arrives next.
To its left the wave is lower, back down the slope.
So the point is about to be lower: it is moving down.
